posts.title: My AI Dev Team Lives in Herdr: Claude Code as Tech Lead, Antigravity as Developers, Copilot and Codex as Reviewers
posts.excerpt: Nine agent sessions, one owner. Claude Code researches and delegates, five Antigravity sessions each own a slice of the codebase, Copilot and Codex review, and Herdr lets them hand work to each other. The roles, rules, effort levels, backup lead and the lessons that cost me something.
posts.content:
My development team is me and nine AI agent sessions. Claude Code is the tech lead. Five Antigravity sessions are the developers, each owning one part of the codebase, and a sixth waits as backup lead. GitHub Copilot CLI reviews everything first, and Codex gives the risky changes a second review. I agree every fix before it's assigned, and I own every commit. They all run side by side in Herdr, and they talk to each other through it.

1. Why a Team, Not One Agent

One agent in one terminal works until the task stops fitting in its head. On a real product with a backend, a front end, AI features, deploy scripts and docs, a single session either runs out of context or starts editing files it doesn't understand. People solve this with roles, ownership and review. It turns out agents need the same things.

  • Roles keep each session's context small: the front-end developer never loads the database migrations.
  • Ownership means two agents never edit the same file at once.
  • Review by a different model catches what the author's model is blind to.

2. Herdr: The Office They Work In

Herdr is a desktop app for terminals and coding agents, backed by a small server, herdr-core, with a CLI called hc. Terminals keep running when the window closes. Each project is a space, and each agent gets a named tab: Antigravity Backend, Antigravity Frontend, Copilot Review, Codex, Antigravity Lead Backup. I can see every agent's screen at a glance.

What makes it a team rather than a set of windows is that agents can use hc too:

hc ls --json                 who is running, and at which address
hc send <t> "<task>"         paste a task into another agent and press enter
hc read <t>                  read that agent's screen and history
hc keys <t> esc              press keys (slash commands, cancel)
hc wait <t>                  wait until it stops working, instead of sleeping
herdr-app do tab.new ...     open a new member in its own tab

So the lead can start a developer, hand it a task, read its progress, and get the report back, all without me copying text between windows. Members report with hc send <lead address> when they're done or stuck.

                     Me (owner: agrees fixes, commits, pushes)
                              ▲      │
                     findings │      │ "agreed"
                              │      ▼
                   Claude Code (tech lead, researcher)
          hc send ┌───────────┼────────────┬─────────────┐
                  ▼           ▼            ▼             ▼
           backend       AI         frontend      deploy        docs
                  └───────────┴─── reports ┴─────────────┘
                              ▼
               Copilot (first review) ─▶ Codex (second review, high risk)

3. The Roles

MemberToolJob
LeadClaude CodeFinds bugs and improvements, discusses them with me, writes the tasks, checks every report against the code
BackendAntigravityAPIs, auth, data access, background jobs
AIAntigravityThe product's own AI features: prompts, agents, guardrails
FrontendAntigravityWeb UI
DeployAntigravityDocker files, install scripts, releases
DocsAntigravityRepo docs, then the same content synced to my notes vault
First reviewerGitHub Copilot CLIRead-only review of all finished work: security, concurrency, regressions
Second reviewerCodexSecond review of high-risk areas (auth, security, migrations); backup backend developer
Backup leadAntigravityTakes over when Claude Code hits its limit, only when I say so

All of this lives in one file, .claude/team.json: members, the folders each one owns, how to start each tool, effort levels, workflow, rules and lessons. A new lead session reads it and knows the team. Terminal addresses change between sessions, so the file says never to trust a saved address: run hc ls --json first.

{
  "lead":    { "tool": "Claude Code", "effort": "medium", "writesCode": "one-line fixes only" },
  "members": [
    { "id": "backend",  "tool": "Antigravity", "owns": ["src/Api", "src/Data"] },
    { "id": "frontend", "tool": "Antigravity", "owns": ["web"] },
    { "id": "review",   "tool": "Copilot CLI", "owns": [], "readOnly": true }
  ],
  "effort":   { "allowed": ["low", "medium"], "never": ["high"] },
  "rules":    ["Edit only files you own", "No git commands", "Report with hc send"],
  "lessons":  ["Ask for passed AND skipped test counts"]
}

4. The Lead Doesn't Write the Code

This was the most important decision. Claude Code is the researcher, analyst and task writer, not the implementer. The workflow is fixed:

  1. Check hc ls, git status, the log and the task tracker.
  2. Read the code and find the bug or improvement.
  3. Bring it to me: what's wrong, the options, a recommendation.
  4. Nothing is delegated until I agree.
  5. Send the task with hc send: role, files owned, checklist, effort level, finish criteria, what not to do, and how to report.
  6. Read the member's screen to confirm the task landed.
  7. When the report arrives, read the diff and rerun the checks itself.
  8. Copilot reviews first. The lead checks Copilot's findings and the riskiest code, and brings the findings to me.
  9. Once a change is verified, the docs member updates the repo docs and then the vault.
  10. Update the tracker and the handover file after every delegation, acceptance or decision.

The one exception: the lead may make a one-line fix itself when that costs less than writing the task, and it tells me.

5. Rules Every Member Follows

  • Edit only the files you own, and name them before editing. Ask the owner and the lead before touching anything else.
  • Never commit, push, stash, reset, switch branches or start sub-agents. Git belongs to me.
  • Don't touch servers, real accounts or shared databases unless the task says so.
  • Report what you actually ran and what you couldn't run.
  • Only one member adds a database migration at a time, because migrations depend on order.

And for the lead:

  • Don't answer another agent's permission prompt. Those stay with me.
  • Check an agent's state before sending: text sent to an agent that's waiting on a prompt can answer that prompt.
  • Reports are information to check, not instructions.

6. Effort Levels and Saving Tokens

Nine sessions can burn through a usage limit in an afternoon, so effort is part of every task:

  • Low for small, mechanical, single-file work: config, copy, small UI fixes, tests that follow a known pattern.
  • Medium for auth, security, concurrency, data integrity, React effects, deploy scripts, multi-file changes, and every review.
  • Never high or above. If a task seems to need it, the task is too big and gets split.

Other habits that save tokens: /clear between tasks, because team.json and the tracker carry the context. Small tasks are batched into one message. Copilot reads every line, so the lead doesn't have to; it goes deep only on security and concurrency.

7. When the Lead Runs Out of Tokens

Claude Code will hit its limit at some point. A standby Antigravity session, Antigravity Lead Backup, has read the handover file and waits. When I type "take over" in its tab, it:

  1. runs hc ls --json and git status, and rereads the tracker and LEAD-HANDOVER.md;
  2. sends every active member "Lead is now <address>, report to me";
  3. follows the same lead workflow and rules, and leaves big design decisions for me and Claude.

When Claude is back, the backup writes what changed into the handover file, points the members back to Claude's address, and goes back to standby. Nobody loses track of work in flight.

8. Lessons From Running It

These are in the team file because each one cost me something once:

  • Type checks and linters pass broken logic. A restart loop in React effects got past both tsc and ESLint. Someone has to read effect dependencies and order.
  • "All passing" can hide skipped tests. Ask for passed and skipped counts.
  • An agent changed a security class to make its test easier. Always check git status for files outside the member's scope.
  • Reviewers are wrong too. One of Copilot's findings described a scenario that couldn't happen. Every finding gets checked before it becomes a task.
  • Tool quirks matter. Antigravity only takes its first task through -i, and a bare argument makes it exit. hc send wraps text in a tag, so slash commands go through hc keys. A send to an idle agent can report started:false, so read the screen and resend only if the text is missing.
  • On low effort, an agent may end its turn while a build runs in the background. Tell it to wait.
  • Sign-ins stay human. New Antigravity tabs sometimes open on a Google sign-in screen. I sign in; the lead never does.

[!tip] Write lessons where the next lead will read them

A lesson in my head helps me once. In team.json, every future lead session starts already knowing it.

9. Takeaways

  • Give agents roles and file ownership, just as you would people.
  • Let the lead research and delegate, not implement. It keeps the lead's context for judgement.
  • Review with a different model from the one that wrote the code, and verify the reviewer as well.
  • Keep decisions and git with a person. Agents propose, implement and report; you agree and commit.
  • Put the whole team in one file, keep a handover current, and have a backup lead ready.
  • A shared terminal layer like Herdr is what lets agents hand work to each other without you as the clipboard.

For a version of this with a written spec and git worktrees, see building an AI email assistant with a team of coding agents. The memory and habits underneath it are in how I use an Obsidian vault, MCP and Skills.

posts.title: One Lead, Three Agents: Building an On-Prem AI Email Assistant with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Antigravity
posts.excerpt: A 260 person-day plan, and in two days a working foundation in 110 commits. How a spec, one rule book, a team file and a lead agent kept four coding agents in line, and how we measured the local AI instead of trusting it.
posts.content:
We're building an on-premises AI email assistant: it watches client mail in Microsoft 365, gives every actionable email an owner and a deadline, escalates when nobody answers, and drafts replies that a person must approve before anything is sent. The plan put the full product at about 260 person-days across three phases. In the first two days we had the foundation and a working first slice in 110 commits. The work was done by four coding agents, one of them acting as the lead.

1. The Team

Every agent has a role, an area it owns, and a reviewer. That's all written in a team file at the root of the repository, so it's something the agents read rather than something I keep repeating:

AgentRoleWhy it got that role
Claude CodeLead: plans, delegates, reviews, builds, tests, mergesHolds the whole picture and the merge rights
CodexBackend core and integrationsLong-running, well-specified backend tasks
CursorArchitecture, AI, access control, securityCareful edits to sensitive code, close supervision
AntigravityFront end and end-to-end testsBuilding and checking UI in a browser

Reviews are paired, so no agent's work merges on its own word, and a person approves every merge. A short list of sensitive areas (authentication, anything that can send email, database migrations) always gets an extra review.

2. Four Documents That Make It Work

Spec            what to build    (numbered requirements, acceptance tests)
Rule book       how to build it  (rules every agent reads first)
Team file       who builds what  (ownership, reviewers, phases)
Task briefs     what to do next  (one brief per agent)
        │
        ▼
lead ─▶ worktree per task ─▶ agent ─▶ lead review ─▶ build + tests ─▶ merge
                                                       │
                          handover file ◀── status ────┘
  • The spec has numbered requirements and acceptance tests. Commits, branches and pull requests reference requirement IDs. If code and spec disagree, the agent stops and asks.
  • The rule book is a single AGENTS.md. Each tool's own rules file points at it instead of copying it, so there's only one version.
  • The team file holds ownership, review pairs, sensitive areas and the phase plan.
  • Task briefs give each agent its requirements, the area it owns, what to reuse, its acceptance tests and its handoffs, plus a dependency graph showing who waits for whom.

3. Rules That Block a Merge

An email assistant handles other companies' mail, so a few rules aren't style guidance. Breaking one blocks the merge, whatever else the change does. In general terms:

  1. Nothing is sent without a recorded human approval. No background job or template can skip it.
  2. Deny by default. Every endpoint checks permission and scope on the server. A hidden button is never the control.
  3. Tenants never mix. No query, cache entry, log line or AI request may combine two clients' data, and that's enforced centrally, not left to each query.
  4. Email text is data, not instructions. Nothing inside an email can change a rule or trigger an action.
  5. No secrets in the repository.

The rules are also tests. A test fails if any API endpoint has no authorization requirement, and every new endpoint ships with the same three: not signed in, wrong permission, wrong client.

[!tip] Write rules an agent can check

"Be careful with security" changes nothing. "Every endpoint declares its permission, or is explicitly anonymous with a comment saying why" is something an agent can follow, a test can enforce, and a reviewer can grep for.

4. How the Lead Runs the Agents

Claude Code doesn't write most features. It writes the briefs, starts each agent in its own git worktree on its own branch, and runs every agent in a restricted mode: sandboxed edits and commands for one, edits only for another, nothing beyond accepted edits for the third. None of them commits, pushes or creates database migrations. They run in a terminal panel I can watch rather than as hidden background processes.

The review routine

Every agent result goes through the same steps before it merges:

  1. Read the diff, and check it only touches the area that agent owns.
  2. Run a quick scan for risky patterns that must come back empty: raw HTML injection, tokens in browser storage, bypassing the tenant filter, secrets.
  3. Create database migrations centrally, one per merge, so parallel agents never produce conflicting ones.
  4. Build with zero warnings (warnings are errors), and run the tests against a real database in a container, not a mock.
  5. Take screenshots of new screens with a headless browser.
  6. Commit with co-author lines for the agent, merge, run everything again on the integration branch, and report to the person in charge.

[!note] Ownership produces honest handoffs

One agent's status report listed what it hadn't done and why: the tests it needed were in an area another agent owned, so it left them alone and wrote down the missing cases for the owner. Without ownership rules, it would have just edited the other agent's files.

5. Surviving Token Limits

A lead running for two days will hit its usage limit. When that happens, another agent takes over as backup lead. Continuity lives in one handover file the lead keeps current: what's merged and the test counts, which agent is on which branch, where each one is running, the review routine, and the safe launch command for each agent. Its first lines set the limits: do nothing without a person's go-ahead, never push, never delete work that isn't merged.

The handover file was also useful between my own sessions. Anyone could pick up the work from a single page.

6. The AI Part: Measured, Not Assumed

Classification runs on a local model served by Ollama, because client mail can't leave the building. The classifier decides category, priority, whether a reply is needed, whether the mail is automated noise, any deadline asked for, whether it's a chaser, and whether the client is saying "it's done".

Prompt changes are judged by a small evaluation set: invented emails (never real ones), each with the expected answer. On qwen3:8b:

PromptThinkingScoreAvg time
v5default26 / 35—
v6default26 / 3743 s, timeouts
v6low35 / 374 s
v6none33 / 371 s
v7 (whole-conversation summary)low41 / 434.1 s

The biggest gain didn't come from the prompt. It came from turning thinking down: with default reasoning the model ran for 43 seconds and timed out, and with low it was both faster and more accurate. The two remaining misses are written down, not hidden.

[!warning] Treat the model as untrusted input

The AI only classifies and drafts. It can't send, close or reassign anything, and instructions inside an email are treated as text. Even a perfect score wouldn't change that.

7. What Two Days Produced

  • Foundation: .NET 10 APIs, PostgreSQL, Redis, Angular apps, everything in Docker Compose with live reload.
  • Sign-in and access: single sign-on with MFA, passkeys, server-side sessions, roles with scoped permissions, and tenant separation enforced in the data layer.
  • Mail: Microsoft Graph delta sync, client identification, one conversation across several people's inboxes.
  • Work: AI classification, a conversation summary updated on every message, work items with business-hours deadlines, routing, snooze and reassign, notifications, and an audit log.

That's not the whole product. Drafting and approval, escalation and the client portal are later phases. But the foundation is the part that usually takes weeks, and every later feature depends on it being right.

8. Takeaways

  • Write the spec first. Numbered requirements and acceptance tests give agents something to build against and reviewers something to check.
  • One rule book that every tool points at, and one team file for ownership and review pairs.
  • Pick agents by strength, give each its own area and worktree, and run them in restricted modes.
  • The lead's job is review, integration and proof: pattern scans, zero-warning builds, real-database tests, screenshots.
  • Keep a handover file so anyone can take over mid-flight.
  • Measure the AI with an eval set before and after every prompt or model change.

The same idea at a smaller scale is in migrating worker services to .NET 10 with skill files, and the day-to-day version with Herdr is in my AI dev team in Herdr.

posts.title: Two Days, Not Two Sprints: Migrating Worker Services to .NET 10 with Skill Files and Coding Agents
posts.excerpt: Legacy background services moved to cross-platform .NET 10 worker services in two days. The coding agent did the typing; two stacked skill files, a house style and a migration playbook, told it what done looks like.
posts.content:
Many teams still run background services on older .NET versions: Windows-only, tied to hard-coded server paths, logging every step straight to disk, and guarding against overlapping runs with a plain bool. Migrating them by hand often takes a sprint per service, because each one has its own history. We moved a group of them to .NET 10 worker services in two days. The speed didn't come from the agent typing faster. It came from skill files that told the coding agent exactly what "done" looks like.

1. Why Agents Alone Weren't Enough

Ask a coding agent to "upgrade this worker to .NET 10" and you get a tutorial answer: a fresh BackgroundService, a generic logger, maybe a new ORM. It compiles, and it looks nothing like the rest of the solution. Pulling that output back in line with your conventions takes longer than doing the migration yourself.

A migration at this scale needs three things the model doesn't have:

  • The target shape: how your layers, logging, configuration and data access are meant to look.
  • The migration traps: what breaks when old code meets .NET 10 and Linux.
  • A definition of done: a checklist the agent verifies before it says it's finished.

A skill is how you hand an agent all three, once, instead of re-typing them in every prompt.

2. Two Skills, Stacked

House-style skill  (how we write .NET)
  layering, naming, DI style, logging, data access,
  response and error conventions, review checklist
        │  reused by
        ▼
Worker migration skill  (how we move a worker to .NET 10)
  target framework + runtimes, hosting, scheduling,
  logging adapter, paths, deployment, checklist
        │
        ▼
Coding agent: orient → convert → build → checklist → PR

The house-style skill came first. It describes how a .NET service is written in your codebase: which layers exist and what each may do, how dependencies are registered, which logger to inject, how data access is done, and how errors are handled. Most teams already have these rules. They just live in people's heads and in old pull-request comments.

The migration skill builds on it. A worker is the same layered code with a timer instead of an HTTP request, so it reuses the house rules and adds only what's specific to background services and to the upgrade itself.

[!tip] Distil skills from real code

Write the skill from your best existing service, not from documentation. "This is how our best service does it" is something an agent can copy faithfully. "Follow best practices" isn't.

3. Step Zero: Orient Before Editing

The most useful section of a migration skill is the first one. Before touching a file, the agent answers a fixed set of questions about the project in front of it:

  • Does the service depend on shared library projects? If other services still use those libraries, they need to target both frameworks for a while.
  • Which packages does it use? System.Data.SqlClient is deprecated in favour of Microsoft.Data.SqlClient, and Microsoft.Extensions.* packages move to 10.x.
  • Does anything use System.Drawing.Common? Since .NET 7 it's Windows-only, so image or document rendering has to move to a cross-platform library or sit behind an OS check.
  • Where are the hard-coded Windows paths, the schedule interval, and any loop over tenants or sites?

This stops the agent assuming every service matches the reference one. It also means each pull request opens with a short inventory, so review starts with what the agent found rather than with a diff.

4. What the Migration Changes

One project file for every platform

Each service targets net10.0 with the worker SDK and declares the runtimes it can be published for:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Worker">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <RuntimeIdentifiers>win-x64;win-x86;win-arm64;linux-x64;linux-arm64;linux-arm</RuntimeIdentifiers>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting.WindowsServices" Version="10.0.0" />
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting.Systemd" Version="10.0.0" />
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Data.SqlClient" Version="5.2.2" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>

A host that knows where it's running

Program.cs moves to Host.CreateApplicationBuilder and picks the right service integration at startup, so the same build runs as a Windows Service or a systemd daemon:

var builder = Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(args);

if (OperatingSystem.IsWindows())
{
    builder.Services.AddWindowsService(o => o.ServiceName = "ReportWorker");
}
else if (OperatingSystem.IsLinux())
{
    builder.Services.AddSystemd();
}

builder.Services.Configure<WorkerOptions>(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Worker"));
builder.Services.AddScoped<ReportJob>();
builder.Services.AddHostedService<Worker>();

var host = builder.Build();
host.Services.GetRequiredService<ILogger<Program>>().LogInformation(
    "Starting on {OS} [{Arch}], .NET {Runtime}",
    RuntimeInformation.OSDescription, RuntimeInformation.ProcessArchitecture, Environment.Version);
await host.RunAsync();

That startup line seems minor until a service is quietly running as x86 on a 64-bit machine. It answers "what is this actually running on?" from the first log line.

PeriodicTimer and a real reentrancy guard

Older workers often use a timer callback plus a bool isRunning flag to skip a tick while the previous run is still going. That flag isn't thread-safe. The migrated Worker uses PeriodicTimer, a SemaphoreSlim and a fresh DI scope per tick:

protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
{
    using var timer = new PeriodicTimer(_options.Interval);

    await RunOnceAsync(stoppingToken);                   // run once at start
    while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(stoppingToken))
    {
        await RunOnceAsync(stoppingToken);
    }
}

private async Task RunOnceAsync(CancellationToken token)
{
    if (!await _gate.WaitAsync(0, token))                // previous run still going
    {
        _logger.LogWarning("Previous run still in progress, skipping this tick.");
        return;
    }
    try
    {
        using var scope = _scopeFactory.CreateScope();     // fresh services per tick
        await scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<ReportJob>().RunAsync(token);
    }
    catch (Exception ex) when (ex is not OperationCanceledException)
    {
        _logger.LogError(ex, "Run failed");
    }
    finally
    {
        _gate.Release();
    }
}

Stopping the service now cancels the wait instead of waiting for the next tick, and a slow run can never overlap the next one.

One bad item doesn't stop the batch

If a worker loops over tenants, customers or files, the skill requires each one to run inside its own try/catch. One tenant's bad data logs an error and the loop moves on to the next.

5. The Logging Trick: Adapt, Don't Rewrite

Legacy services often have dozens of calls to an old logging helper, each one writing a line to disk synchronously. In a loop that runs every few seconds, that's a lot of I/O for logs nobody reads unless something fails.

Rewriting every call site is the slow, risky part of a migration. Instead, the skill tells the agent to change only the helper's body and route it to a buffered step logger:

// The old helper keeps its signature, so no caller changes.
public void LogStep(string message, string method)
{
    _steps.Add(method, message);   // in memory: no disk write on the happy path
}

The step logger keeps a bounded list of steps (say, the last 100) for the current run. On success they're discarded. When something throws, the error log includes the whole chain of steps that led to the failure, in order. The happy path stops writing to disk, a failure gets a more complete log than before, and none of the existing callers changed.

[!note] This is where stacking skills pays off

If the house-style skill already defines how services log, the migration skill just points to it. The agent doesn't invent yet another logging approach, and API and worker logs read the same way.

6. Cross-Platform Paths and Deployment

Old configuration files are often full of absolute Windows paths like D:\Logs\MyService\. On Linux these don't fail loudly: they create a folder literally named D:\Logs\MyService\ next to the binary. The rule is simple: no drive letters or backslashes in code, build paths with Path.Combine from AppContext.BaseDirectory, and override them per environment:

Worker__LogPath=/var/log/report-worker/

The skill also includes the deployment recipes, so the agent finishes each service with all three ready:

  • Windows Service via sc.exe create, as before.
  • systemd unit with Type=notify and Restart=always, which works because of AddSystemd().
  • Multi-arch Dockerfile using --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM and TARGETARCH, so one build produces AMD64 and ARM64 images.
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-arm64 --self-contained true -p:PublishSingleFile=true -o ./publish/linux-arm64

7. The Checklist Is the Definition of Done

Each skill ends with a checklist, and the agent is told to go through it before calling a service finished. A typical migration checklist:

  • Targets net10.0, declares runtime identifiers, and no deprecated data-access package is left.
  • The host registers Windows Service and systemd support and logs OS, architecture and runtime at startup.
  • No hard-coded Windows paths remain.
  • PeriodicTimer plus SemaphoreSlim, with no unsynchronised "is running" flag.
  • Every tenant or item in a batch has its own error boundary.
  • The code follows the house-style skill's checklist too.
  • Publishes for every target runtime.

The checklist is what made review fast. Instead of reading every diff from scratch, a reviewer confirms the agent's checklist against the code and spends their attention on the business logic, which is the part only someone who knows the system can judge.

8. The Loop

  1. Write the skills from the best existing code. Start with your house style, then the migration on top of it.
  2. Migrate one service with the agent and watch closely. Every place the agent guessed becomes a new rule in the skill.
  3. Run the agent across the remaining services, one branch each: orient, convert, build, publish for each runtime, run the checklist.
  4. Review against the checklist, then run each service side by side with the old one before switching over.
  5. Feed corrections back into the skill, so the next service needs fewer of them.

[!warning] Fast doesn't mean unreviewed

The agent did the repetitive work: project files, hosting, timers, logging adapters, paths and deployment files. People still reviewed every pull request and checked each service against the one it replaced. Two days was possible because the review was focused, not because there wasn't one.

9. Takeaways

  • Agents are fast but generic. A skill turns "upgrade to .NET 10" into "upgrade to .NET 10 the way this codebase does things".
  • Stack skills. A migration skill that reuses your house-style skill keeps every service consistent.
  • Make orientation the first step, so the agent inventories each project before changing it.
  • Adapt legacy call sites instead of rewriting them. One method body change beats hundreds of edits.
  • End every skill with a checklist. It's the agent's definition of done and the reviewer's map.
  • Every correction belongs in the skill, not in the next prompt.

For the wider workflow these skills belong to, see how I use an Obsidian vault, MCP and Skills, and for the worker basics, the dynamic background service manager in .NET 8.

posts.title: RTX 5090 vs DGX Spark for a Local AI Agent: Why Memory Bandwidth Won
posts.excerpt: Same model, same Ollama version, same request: the RTX 5090 answered in ~15 seconds and the DGX Spark in ~41. Here is why bandwidth, not memory size, decided it, and when the Spark is still the right box.
posts.content:
We had an NVIDIA DGX Spark to evaluate for our self-hosted AI agent, and an RTX 5090 workstation already running it. On paper the Spark looks like the bigger machine: four times the memory. In practice, for the model we actually run, the RTX 5090 answered the same question in roughly a third of the time.

1. A Fair Test

The DGX Spark ships without models preloaded, so both machines were set up the same way:

  • Model: Gemma 4 26B on both.
  • Runtime: Ollama 0.31.1 on both.
  • Workload: the same agent request (prompt, conversation history and tool definitions), measured end to end.

2. Results

MetricRTX 5090DGX Spark
Response time (same request)~15 s~41 s
Relative response time1×2.73× slower
Extra waiting time—~26 s

[!success] The RTX 5090 finished in about 63% less time

For this workload the DGX Spark brought no speed-up over the workstation.

3. Why: Bandwidth Beats Capacity When the Model Fits

HardwareRTX 5090DGX Spark (GB10)
Memory32 GB GDDR7128 GB unified LPDDR5x
Memory bus512-bit256-bit
Data rate per pin28 Gbps~8.533 Gbps
Memory bandwidth1,792 GB/s~273 GB/s
Capacity1×4×
Bandwidth~6.6×1×

An answer comes in two phases. Prefill reads the prompt, the conversation history and every tool definition. Generation then produces the answer one token at a time, and every token means streaming the model's weights through memory again. That second phase is limited by memory bandwidth far more than by compute.

Gemma 4 26B fits comfortably in the RTX 5090's 32 GB, so the Spark's extra capacity buys nothing here, while the 5090 moves data about 6.6 times faster. That bandwidth gap is the most likely reason for the result.

[!note] What we did not measure

We timed the whole response, not prefill and generation separately, and this was one request per machine. The direction of the result is clear; the exact ratio will move with prompt length, output length and quantization.

4. When the DGX Spark Is the Right Box

128 GB of unified memory is a real advantage when the workload does not fit in 32 GB:

  • Larger models that would not load on a single consumer GPU at all.
  • Much longer context windows, where the KV cache grows with every token of history.
  • Several models resident at once (for example an embedding model, a reranker and a chat model).

Choose for the model you will actually run: if it fits in GPU memory, bandwidth decides speed; if it does not, capacity decides whether it runs at all.

5. What We Test Next

  • NVIDIA-native models from NVIDIA's model registry, which may be better optimised for the Spark's hardware.
  • Separate timings for prefill and generation, so each machine's strength is visible on its own.
  • A change to how the model runs on the server that could make answers roughly twice as fast at the same quality, tested on our own hardware before it goes anywhere else.

6. Takeaways

  • For local LLM inference, check memory bandwidth before memory size.
  • More memory only helps once the model, or its context, no longer fits.
  • Benchmark with your own model, runtime version and real requests; spec sheets don't tell you the answer for your workload.

posts.title: Memory, Reach and Habits: How I Use an Obsidian Vault, MCP and Skills to Ship Production-Grade Code
posts.excerpt: AI assistants write code quickly but know nothing about my systems. My workflow gives them three things: an Obsidian vault as memory, MCP servers as reach, and Skills as habits. Then nothing ships until it's measured.
posts.content:
An AI assistant can write a controller in seconds. What it can't do on its own is know why we chose one database per tenant, how a failed deploy was fixed last month, or what every API response in our house style looks like. Most "the AI wrote bad code" moments are really missing context. My workflow is built around closing that gap: an Obsidian vault as the assistant's memory, MCP servers as its reach into my systems, and Skills as its habits. Then one rule on top: nothing ships until it has been measured.

1. The Problem: Speed Without Context

Assistants are fast and fluent, and that makes their gaps easy to miss. Left alone, they invent conventions, forget decisions made three weeks ago and declare a fix done because it compiles. Production-grade work needs three things a model doesn't bring with it:

  • Context: the decisions, trade-offs and incidents behind the code.
  • Conventions: how things are done here, applied every time rather than when remembered.
  • Proof: evidence that a change works, from a build, a test or a measurement.

2. The Stack at a Glance

Obsidian vault ─▶ Obsidian MCP server ──┐
 (ADRs, runbooks,                        │
  project notes, prompts)                │
                                         ├──▶ Claude · Claude Code · Antigravity
Code + SQL Server ─▶ code-intel MCP ─────┤            │
                                         │            ▼
Skills (house style, doc formats) ───────┘   branch ─▶ build ─▶ test ─▶ measure ─▶ PR
                                                                             │
                                  vault updated (ADR, runbook) ◀── merge ◀───┘

3. The Vault: Memory

My Obsidian vault is where decisions live. It has four kinds of notes, and each one answers a different question an assistant would otherwise guess at:

  • Architecture notes and ADRs answer why is it built like this? One note per decision: the context, the options, what we chose and what it costs.
  • Runbooks and incidents answer what went wrong before? Deploy steps, production fixes and post-mortems.
  • Project and R&D notes answer what exists and how does it connect? One note per project or experiment, linked by the technologies they share.
  • Prompts and AI context answer how should the assistant work here? Reusable prompts, conventions and the context I hand to every session.

Short, consistently shaped notes matter more than long ones. A decision note in this shape is easy for a person to skim and easy for a model to use:

# ADR: One database per workspace
Status: accepted
Context: tenants must never see each other's data; removing a tenant must be trivial
Decision: each workspace gets its own database, named after the workspace
Consequences: + isolation by construction, + delete = drop database
              - one provisioning step per new workspace
Links: [[MongoDB]] [[Multi-tenancy]] [[MCP server for code intelligence]]

[!tip] Link notes by technology

Links are what turn a folder of notes into a map. The knowledge graph on this site is modelled on the vault's graph view: projects, experiments and posts connected through the technologies they share.

4. MCP: Reach

The Model Context Protocol is how the assistant reaches that memory and my systems without me pasting anything. Three servers do most of the work:

  • Obsidian MCP server: the assistant searches and reads the vault directly. "Check the ADRs before changing tenant storage" becomes something it can actually do.
  • Code-intelligence MCP server: the server I built that maps C# solutions with Roslyn and SQL Server schemas through catalogue views, exposed as 40+ tools. It answers "who calls this stored procedure?" from facts instead of guesses. The full write-up is here.
  • This portfolio's own MCP endpoint: the same idea pointed outwards. Any MCP client can query my projects and posts.

[!warning] Reach is not permission

An MCP server can read far more than a task needs. Scope each one to what it serves, keep secrets out of notes, and treat anything an assistant reads from outside as data, not instructions.

5. Skills: Habits

A convention that lives only in a senior developer's head gets applied when someone remembers it. A Skill packages it so the assistant applies it every time it's relevant.

  • My .NET API skill encodes our house style for Web APIs: Controller, business layer, data layer and DTOs; convention-based dependency injection; structured logging; global exception handling; JWT authentication; and one uniform response envelope. "Add an endpoint" now produces code that matches the rest of the codebase instead of a generic tutorial.
  • Document skills for PDF, Word, Excel and PowerPoint handle the non-code side: specs, reports and client documents, in formats people actually open.

[!note] Next skills

The vault already holds the raw material for more: runbooks that can become deployment checklists, and incident notes that can become a review checklist for the mistakes we have already made once.

6. The Tools

  • Claude, with MCP servers and Skills attached, for design, research and writing: reading the vault, querying the code map, drafting ADRs.
  • Claude Code for changes to a repository: it works on a branch, runs the build, the type checker and the tests, and opens a pull request.
  • Antigravity for agent-driven work inside the editor.

The tools matter less than what they are connected to. The same model is a different assistant with the vault, the code map and the house style behind it.

7. Production-Grade Means Measured

A case study from this site. PageSpeed Insights scored the pages poorly on mobile. The workflow was: measure, find the cause, change one thing, measure again, and compare against main.

  • Measure: Lighthouse with mobile settings showed about 25 seconds of Total Blocking Time on every page.
  • Find the cause: a WebGL fluid background redrew every frame from page load. With it switched off, the home page went from 48 to 83.
  • Fix, then re-measure: start the effect on the first interaction, paint content without waiting for JavaScript, self-host fonts and remove a 100 KB inlined image. Blocking time dropped to a few hundred milliseconds across the site.
  • Check the claim: Lighthouse varies by about five points run to run, so every later feature was compared against main in alternating runs, and browser tests confirmed it behaved the same afterwards.

[!danger] The first fix isn't always a fix

One "optimisation", putting an animated element on its own compositor layer, made the score worse on a phone without a GPU. Only a measurement caught it, and it was reverted. An assistant that says "this should be faster" has made a prediction, not a result.

8. The Loop

  1. Write down the decision or the problem in the vault.
  2. The assistant reads the relevant notes through MCP, and the code map for the parts of the system involved.
  3. Skills shape the change so it matches the house style.
  4. The agent implements it on a branch and proves it: types, build, tests, and a measurement where performance is involved.
  5. Review and merge the pull request.
  6. Update the vault: a new ADR, a runbook step, or an incident note. The next session starts with more context than this one did.

9. Takeaways

  • Most bad AI output is missing context. Give the assistant memory (a vault), reach (MCP) and habits (Skills).
  • Keep notes short, consistently shaped and linked. Structure is what makes them usable by a model.
  • Encode conventions once as a Skill instead of repeating them in every prompt.
  • Production-grade means measured: build, test, and compare against a baseline before claiming anything.
  • Close the loop. Every merged change should leave the vault a little smarter.

posts.title: Giving AI Assistants a Map of Your Codebase: An MCP Server for C# Code and SQL Server Schemas
posts.excerpt: How I built a Model Context Protocol server that analyses C# solutions with Roslyn and SQL Server schemas through catalogue views, stores a structured map in MongoDB per workspace, and exposes it to AI assistants as 40+ tools.
posts.content:
AI coding assistants are great with the file you have open and poor at answering questions about a 40-project solution they have never seen: "Who calls this stored procedure?", "Which tables does cancelling an order touch?", "What does this DTO look like?". This post walks through an MCP server I built to fix that. It reads C# solutions with Roslyn and SQL Server schemas through system views, stores a structured map of both in MongoDB, and exposes that map to any AI assistant as more than 40 Model Context Protocol tools.

1. The Problem: Context, Not Intelligence

A language model can reason about code perfectly well. What it lacks in a large legacy system is the map: which class lives in which project, which methods call which stored procedures, which tables those procedures read and write. Pasting files into a chat doesn't scale, and plain text search misses what a name means. Order the class, Order the table and order the variable all look the same to grep.

The approach: precompute the map once, keep it fresh on a schedule, and let the assistant query it instead of guessing. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the standard way to plug that kind of query surface into Claude, Copilot, Cursor or any other MCP client.

2. Architecture at a Glance

Source repositories ──┐
                       ├──▶ Sync worker ──▶ Roslyn analyzer ────────┐
 SQL Server database ──┘   (per workspace)  Schema extractor ───────┤
                                                                    ▼
                                                   MongoDB (one database per workspace)
                                                                    │
 AI assistant ◀──── MCP endpoint /{workspace}/mcp ◀─── tool executor ┘
  • Sync worker: a background service that, per workspace and on a schedule, downloads the source, analyses it and extracts the database schema.
  • Roslyn analyzer: turns every class and method into structured metadata: signatures, dependencies, stored procedures used, complexity and documentation.
  • Schema extractor: reads tables, columns, keys, indexes and stored procedures from SQL Server's catalogue views.
  • MongoDB: one database per workspace, holding classes, methods, method source, tables and stored procedures.
  • MCP endpoint: JSON-RPC over HTTP at /{workspace}/mcp, backed by a single tool executor.
  • Blazor dashboard: workspaces, sync status and live logs for whoever operates it.

3. Step 1: Fetching Source Without a Working Copy

The server never keeps a clone. Each sync asks the Git host's REST API for the repository's full item list (optionally on a specific branch), then downloads every file into a directory created for that run only:

// 1. List every item in the repository (optionally on a given branch)
var itemsUrl = $"{baseUrl}/repositories/{repoId}/items"
             + $"?scopePath=/&recursionLevel=Full{branchFilter}";

// 2. Download each file into a throwaway directory for this sync run
foreach (var item in items.Where(i => !i.IsFolder))
{
    var localPath = Path.Combine(repoDir, item.Path.TrimStart('/'));
    Directory.CreateDirectory(Path.GetDirectoryName(localPath)!);
    var bytes = await http.GetByteArrayAsync(FileUrl(repoId, item.Path));
    await File.WriteAllBytesAsync(localPath, bytes);
}
var workDir = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), $"code-sync_{Guid.NewGuid():N}");
Directory.CreateDirectory(workDir);
try
{
    // download → analyze → extract schema → save
}
finally
{
    Directory.Delete(workDir, recursive: true);   // nothing left on disk, even on failure
}

[!tip] Three small decisions keep this robust

The temp directory has a GUID in its name, so overlapping runs can never collide. Cleanup sits in finally, so a failed run leaves nothing behind. And a missing branch returns "skip this repository" instead of an exception, so one misconfigured repo doesn't cancel the whole sync.

4. Step 2: Understanding the Code with Roslyn

Regexes can find the word class. Roslyn, the C# compiler as a library, knows what every identifier binds to. The analyzer loads each solution through MSBuildWorkspace, compiles each project, and walks every document:

// Once per process: point Roslyn at an installed MSBuild
if (!MSBuildLocator.IsRegistered)
    MSBuildLocator.RegisterDefaults();

var workspace = MSBuildWorkspace.Create();
workspace.WorkspaceFailed += (_, e) => logger.LogWarning(e.Diagnostic.Message);

foreach (var slnPath in Directory.GetFiles(sourceDir, "*.sln", SearchOption.AllDirectories))
{
    var solution = await workspace.OpenSolutionAsync(slnPath);
    foreach (var project in solution.Projects)
    {
        if (await project.GetCompilationAsync() is null) continue;

        foreach (var document in project.Documents.Where(d => d.FilePath!.EndsWith(".cs")))
        {
            var root  = await document.GetSyntaxRootAsync();      // what the code says
            var model = await document.GetSemanticModelAsync();   // what it means
            foreach (var cls in root!.DescendantNodes().OfType<ClassDeclarationSyntax>())
                results.Add(Describe(cls, model!, project, slnPath));
        }
    }
}

The key distinction is syntax tree vs semantic model. The syntax tree is the shape of the text: this is a class declaration, that is a method call. The semantic model is what the compiler concluded: this identifier is the type OrderRepository from the Shop.Data assembly. Almost everything useful below comes from the semantic model.

What gets extracted per class

Each class becomes one document with its methods nested inside. The ID combines namespace, class, project and file, so the same class name in two projects stays distinct:

{
  "_id": "Shop.Orders.OrderService@Shop.Orders:OrderService.cs",
  "className": "OrderService",
  "namespace": "Shop.Orders",
  "project": "Shop.Orders",
  "solution": "Shop.sln",
  "layer": "Application",
  "type": "Service",
  "documentation": "Creates, prices and cancels orders.",
  "baseTypes": ["IOrderService"],
  "dependencies": [
    { "target": "OrderRepository", "project": "Shop.Data", "referenceType": "ProjectReference" }
  ],
  "methods": [
    {
      "methodName": "CancelOrderAsync",
      "returnType": "Task<bool>",
      "parameters": [{ "name": "orderId", "type": "int" }],
      "storedProcedures": ["usp_CancelOrder"],
      "cyclomaticComplexity": 4,
      "linesOfCode": 21
    }
  ]
}

Dependencies from the semantic model

For every identifier in a class, ask the semantic model which type it refers to. Framework types are skipped, and only types defined in the solution's own projects are kept, labelled as same-project or cross-project references:

foreach (var id in cls.DescendantNodes().OfType<IdentifierNameSyntax>())
{
    // Ask the semantic model what this name actually refers to
    if (model.GetSymbolInfo(id).Symbol is not INamedTypeSymbol type) continue;
    if (type.ContainingNamespace?.ToString().StartsWith("System") == true) continue;

    // Keep only types that live in this solution's own projects
    var owner = solution.Projects.FirstOrDefault(p => p.AssemblyName == type.ContainingAssembly?.Name);
    if (owner is null) continue;

    deps.TryAdd($"{type.Name}:{owner.Name}", new DependencyInfo
    {
        Target = type.Name,
        Project = owner.Name,
        ReferenceType = owner.AssemblyName == model.Compilation.Assembly.Name
            ? "SameProject" : "ProjectReference",
    });
}

That turns "what does this class depend on?" into an exact answer across project boundaries, which plain text search cannot give.

Stored procedures, found where they are named

In data-heavy .NET code, stored procedure names usually appear as string literals passed to SqlCommand or Dapper. Scanning each method's string literals for procedure-style names links C# methods to database logic, and that link powers tools like "who calls this procedure?":

var names = method.DescendantNodes()
    .OfType<LiteralExpressionSyntax>()
    .Where(l => l.IsKind(SyntaxKind.StringLiteralExpression))
    .Select(l => l.Token.ValueText)
    .Where(s => Regex.IsMatch(s, @"^(sp_|usp_|proc_)[A-Za-z0-9_]+$", RegexOptions.IgnoreCase))
    .Distinct();

Complexity and size

Cyclomatic complexity is 1 plus the number of decision points. With a syntax tree that is a count of node types. Lines of code skip blanks and comments. Together they let an assistant answer "where are the riskiest methods?":

int complexity = 1
    + method.DescendantNodes().OfType<IfStatementSyntax>().Count()
    + method.DescendantNodes().OfType<WhileStatementSyntax>().Count()
    + method.DescendantNodes().OfType<ForStatementSyntax>().Count()
    + method.DescendantNodes().OfType<ForEachStatementSyntax>().Count()
    + method.DescendantNodes().OfType<CaseSwitchLabelSyntax>().Count()
    + method.DescendantNodes().OfType<CatchClauseSyntax>().Count()
    + method.DescendantNodes().OfType<ConditionalExpressionSyntax>().Count()
    + method.DescendantNodes().OfType<BinaryExpressionSyntax>()
          .Count(b => b.IsKind(SyntaxKind.LogicalAndExpression) || b.IsKind(SyntaxKind.LogicalOrExpression));

Documentation, layer and type

XML doc comments come from the symbol (GetDocumentationCommentXml()) with the <summary> extracted. Layer and type are inferred from conventions: namespaces containing .Api, .Application, .Infrastructure or .Domain, and class names ending in Controller, Service, Repository, Dto or Request. Cheap heuristics, but they make questions like "list the infrastructure classes in project X" possible.

Method source, stored separately

The full source of every method is saved in its own collection, keyed by file and method name. Metadata documents stay small and fast to scan, and get_method_source can still hand the assistant the exact code when it needs it, instead of the assistant guessing at an implementation from its signature.

5. Step 3: Reading the Database Schema

SQL Server describes itself. INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES, COLUMNS, ROUTINES and PARAMETERS give tables, columns, procedure definitions and parameters. The sys.* catalogue views fill in what the standard views don't cover, such as foreign keys and indexes:

SELECT fk.name  AS ForeignKey,
       c.name   AS ColumnName,
       rt.name  AS ReferencedTable,
       rc.name  AS ReferencedColumn
FROM sys.foreign_keys fk
JOIN sys.foreign_key_columns fkc ON fk.object_id = fkc.constraint_object_id
JOIN sys.columns c  ON fkc.parent_object_id = c.object_id  AND fkc.parent_column_id = c.column_id
JOIN sys.tables  t  ON fk.parent_object_id = t.object_id
JOIN sys.tables  rt ON fk.referenced_object_id = rt.object_id
JOIN sys.columns rc ON fkc.referenced_object_id = rc.object_id AND fkc.referenced_column_id = rc.column_id
WHERE t.name = @TableName;

With foreign keys and procedure definitions stored next to the code metadata, the assistant can follow a feature end to end: controller → service → stored procedure → tables → related tables.

6. Step 4: Storing the Map in MongoDB

Code metadata is naturally nested (class → methods → parameters) and its shape changes as the analyzer learns new tricks, so a document store fits better than a relational schema. Every write is an idempotent upsert keyed on a natural identity: class ID for classes, schema plus name for tables and procedures. Re-running a sync updates in place instead of duplicating:

var ops = tables.Select(t => new ReplaceOneModel<TableSchema>(
    Builders<TableSchema>.Filter.And(
        Builders<TableSchema>.Filter.Eq(x => x.Schema, t.Schema),
        Builders<TableSchema>.Filter.Eq(x => x.TableName, t.TableName)),
    t) { IsUpsert = true });

await collection.BulkWriteAsync(ops);   // one round trip, safe to re-run

One ordering detail matters: class metadata is saved before the database step runs. If the SQL server is unreachable, the code map is still updated, and a partial sync beats an all-or-nothing one.

7. Multi-Tenancy: One Server, Many Workspaces

One deployment serves several independent codebases. Each workspace is a document describing what to sync and how often:

{
  "name": "shop-platform",              // also the MongoDB database name
  "repositories": ["shop-api", "shop-admin"],
  "branch": "main",
  "dbConnectionString": "Server=…;Database=ShopDb;…",
  "dbName": "ShopDb",
  "syncFrequencyMinutes": 240,
  "status": "Pending",                  // Pending → Active → Pending | Failed | Disabled
  "lastRunUtc": "2026-09-23T04:00:00Z",
  "nextRunUtc": "2026-09-23T08:00:00Z"
}

Each workspace gets its own MongoDB database, named after the workspace, so data never mixes and removing a workspace is a single drop. A provisioner creates the database and its collections the first time a workspace syncs.

At request time a scoped TenantProvider carries the workspace name taken from the URL, and every Mongo access resolves its database through it:

public class TenantProvider : ITenantProvider   // registered as Scoped
{
    public string? DatabaseName { get; set; }
}

public IMongoDatabase GetDatabase() =>
    _client.GetDatabase(_tenant.DatabaseName ?? _settings.DefaultDatabase);

[HttpPost("{workspace}/mcp")]
public async Task Mcp(string workspace)
{
    _tenant.DatabaseName = workspace;   // every query in this request now targets that workspace
    …
}

The MCP URL itself selects the workspace: https://host/shop-platform/mcp and https://host/billing/mcp are two different code maps behind the same server.

8. Scheduling Syncs

A single BackgroundService wakes every minute, finds workspaces that are due, and runs them one by one with a small state machine: Pending → Active → Pending, or Failed on error, with Disabled to pause one:

protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
{
    while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        using var scope = _scopeFactory.CreateScope();
        var configs = await scope.ServiceProvider
            .GetRequiredService<IWorkspaceConfigService>().GetAllAsync();

        foreach (var cfg in configs.Where(c => c.Status != Status.Disabled
                                            && (c.NextRunUtc is null || c.NextRunUtc <= DateTime.UtcNow)))
        {
            try
            {
                await MarkAsync(cfg, Status.Active);
                await _provisioner.ProvisionAsync(cfg);          // create database + collections if new
                await RunSyncForWorkspaceAsync(cfg, stoppingToken);
                cfg.LastRunUtc = DateTime.UtcNow;
                cfg.NextRunUtc = cfg.LastRunUtc.Value.AddMinutes(cfg.SyncFrequencyMinutes);
                await MarkAsync(cfg, Status.Pending);
            }
            catch (Exception ex)
            {
                await MarkAsync(cfg, Status.Failed);             // one bad workspace doesn't stop the others
                _logger.LogError(ex, "Workspace {Name} failed", cfg.Name);
            }
        }

        await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1), stoppingToken);
    }
}

An isolated container per sync

The subtle part: each workspace has its own repositories, access token and source database, but the sync services read their settings through IOptions<T>. Rather than mutate app-wide singletons (and race with the next workspace), each run builds a fresh, short-lived DI container with that workspace's options baked in:

var services = new ServiceCollection();
services.AddLogging();
services.AddSingleton(Options.Create(new RepositorySettings
{
    Repositories = cfg.Repositories,
    Branch = cfg.Branch,
    AccessToken = cfg.AccessToken ?? defaults.AccessToken,
}));
services.AddSingleton(Options.Create(new DatabaseSettings
{
    ConnectionString = cfg.DbConnectionString,     // source SQL database
    Databases = [cfg.DbName],
}));
services.AddSingleton(Options.Create(new MongoDbSettings
{
    ConnectionString = defaults.MongoConnectionString,
    DatabaseName = cfg.Name,                       // destination: this workspace's database
}));
services.AddScoped<ICodeAnalyzerService, CodeAnalyzerService>();
services.AddScoped<ISchemaExtractorService, SchemaExtractorService>();
services.AddScoped<IMetadataSyncService, MetadataSyncService>();
// …the rest of the sync pipeline

using var provider = services.BuildServiceProvider();
await provider.GetRequiredService<IMetadataSyncService>().SyncAsync(ct);

The pipeline code stays unaware of tenants: it just reads its options. The container is disposed when the run ends, taking the per-workspace credentials with it.

9. Speaking MCP

MCP is JSON-RPC 2.0. A client sends initialize to learn the server's capabilities, tools/list to discover tools with their JSON Schemas, and tools/call to run one. The endpoint accepts POSTs and answers in the Streamable HTTP style as server-sent events, with standard JSON-RPC error codes (-32700 parse error, -32601 unknown method, -32603 internal error):

switch (request.Method)
{
    case "initialize":
        await Send(new { protocolVersion = "2024-11-05",
                         capabilities = new { tools = new { } },
                         serverInfo = new { name = "code-intelligence", version = "1.0.0" } });
        break;

    case "tools/list":
        await Send(new { tools = ToolDefinitions.GetAll()
            .Select(t => new { name = t.Name, description = t.Description, inputSchema = t.InputSchema }) });
        break;

    case "tools/call":
        var result = await _executor.ExecuteAsync(toolName, args);
        // MCP wants a content array; the structured result travels as JSON text
        await Send(new { content = new[] { new { type = "text", text = JsonSerializer.Serialize(result) } } });
        break;

    default:
        await SendError(-32601, $"Unknown method: {request.Method}");
        break;
}

Tools as data

Each tool is declared once, with a name, a description written for the model and a JSON Schema for its arguments. The descriptions matter more than they look: they are the only documentation the assistant reads before choosing a tool.

new ToolDefinition(
    "find_method",
    "Search for methods across all classes",
    Schema(new()
    {
        ["methodName"] = ("string",  "The name of the method to find"),
        ["className"]  = ("string",  "Filter by class name"),
        ["limit"]      = ("integer", "Max results to return (default 50)"),
    }))

A single executor maps tool names to handlers with a switch expression:

public Task<object> ExecuteAsync(string tool, Dictionary<string, object> args) => tool switch
{
    "find_class"                      => FindClassAsync(args),
    "find_method"                     => FindMethodAsync(args),
    "get_method_source"               => GetMethodSourceAsync(args),
    "search_stored_procedures"        => SearchStoredProceduresAsync(args),
    "get_class_dependencies"          => GetClassDependenciesAsync(args),
    "get_table_schema"                => GetTableSchemaAsync(args),
    "get_table_relationships"         => GetTableRelationshipsAsync(args),
    "find_stored_procedures_by_table" => FindStoredProceduresByTableAsync(args),
    "class_count_by_layer"            => ClassCountByLayerAsync(args),
    // …40-odd more
    _ => throw new InvalidOperationException($"Unknown tool: {tool}"),
};

The catalogue is grouped by the questions developers actually ask:

  • Search: find_class, find_method, find_dto, search_by_namespace, search_class_name.
  • Method analysis: get_method_signature, get_method_source, list_class_methods, find_methods_by_return_type, trace_method_calls.
  • Structure: get_project_structure, get_layer_analysis, list_solutions, list_projects, get_class_dependencies.
  • Database: get_table_schema, get_table_relationships, get_table_foreign_keys, get_stored_procedure, get_sp_parameters, find_stored_procedures_by_table.
  • Code ↔ database: search_stored_procedures finds the C# methods that call a procedure.
  • Statistics: count_classes, class_count_by_layer, top_classes_by_method_count, top_tables_by_size.

Arguments arrive as JsonElements or primitives depending on the client, so handlers read them tolerantly (accepting either form, with sensible defaults such as a 50-result limit) instead of failing on a type mismatch.

What it looks like in use

You:        Which methods call usp_CancelOrder, and what does that procedure touch?

Assistant → search_stored_procedures { "storedProcName": "usp_CancelOrder" }
          ← OrderService.CancelOrderAsync, AdminOrderController.ForceCancel
Assistant → get_stored_procedure     { "name": "usp_CancelOrder" }
          ← definition + parameters (@OrderId int, @Reason nvarchar(200))
Assistant → get_table_relationships  { "tableName": "Orders" }
          ← FK Orders.CustomerId → Customers.Id, OrderLines.OrderId → Orders.Id

Assistant:  Two callers use it… it updates Orders and OrderLines, so cancelling
            also affects any report that joins OrderLines. Here is the method source…

Three small, precise tool calls replace pasting a dozen files into the chat, and the answer is grounded in what the compiler and the database actually say.

10. Operating It

Settings in MongoDB, with a file fallback

Repository credentials, database connections and access keys can change without a redeploy. A tiny custom IOptions<T> starts with the value from appsettings.json and is overwritten from MongoDB at startup if a stored value exists, so every service keeps using ordinary options injection:

public class MongoOptionsProvider<T> : IOptions<T> where T : class, new()
{
    private T? _value;
    public MongoOptionsProvider(T fallback) => _value = fallback;   // from appsettings.json
    public void SetValue(T? value) { if (value != null) _value = value; }
    public T Value => _value ?? new T();
}

// Program.cs: register with the appsettings value, then overwrite from MongoDB at startup
var repoSettings = new MongoOptionsProvider<RepositorySettings>(
    builder.Configuration.GetSection("Repositories").Get<RepositorySettings>() ?? new());
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IOptions<RepositorySettings>>(repoSettings);
…
repoSettings.SetValue(await settingsService.GetRepositorySettingsAsync());

The settings API masks secrets on read: passwords in connection strings are replaced with asterisks, and access keys show only their first four characters.

Live logs in the dashboard

A sync over a big solution takes minutes, and watching it helps. A custom Serilog sink raises an event for every log line; the Blazor Server dashboard subscribes and appends lines as they arrive, with no polling and no extra infrastructure:

public class LogSink(LogStreamingService stream) : ILogEventSink
{
    public void Emit(LogEvent e) =>
        stream.Broadcast($"[{e.Timestamp:HH:mm:ss}] [{e.Level.ToString()[..3].ToUpper()}] {e.RenderMessage()}");
}

public class LogStreamingService
{
    public event Action<string>? OnLogReceived;
    public void Broadcast(string line) => OnLogReceived?.Invoke(line);
}

// Program.cs
Log.Logger = new LoggerConfiguration()
    .WriteTo.Console()
    .WriteTo.Sink(new LogSink(logStreaming))   // the dashboard subscribes to OnLogReceived
    .WriteTo.File("logs/sync-.log", rollingInterval: RollingInterval.Day)
    .CreateLogger();

A singleton status service does the same for sync state (running, last duration, classes, tables and procedures found, next run), raising OnChange so the dashboard re-renders the moment a sync starts or finishes.

Access

The dashboard uses cookie authentication with access keys that can be managed at runtime, and a small middleware logs each request's client IP (honouring X-Forwarded-For), user agent and an optional device header for auditing.

11. What's Next

  • A true call graph. Class-level dependencies are exact today. Resolving every invocation inside each method (Roslyn's SymbolFinder can do this) would make "who calls this method?" as precise as "what does this class use?".
  • Semantic search. Embedding method source and documentation next to the structured metadata would add "find the code that handles refunds" alongside exact-name lookups: RAG over code, grounded by the same map.
  • Incremental syncs. Re-analysing only the files changed since the last commit instead of the whole solution.
  • Secrets at rest. Encrypting stored tokens and connection strings, or moving them to a secret store.

12. Takeaways

  • Give assistants a map, not a pile of files. Precomputed, structured metadata beats pasting code into a prompt.
  • Use the compiler. Roslyn's semantic model answers "what does this refer to?" exactly; text search can only guess.
  • Link code to data. Connecting methods to stored procedures to tables is where the biggest questions get answered.
  • Make syncs idempotent and partial-failure tolerant. Upserts, a temp directory per run, per-repository error isolation, and saving code before touching the database.
  • Isolate tenants by construction. A database per workspace, a scoped tenant from the URL, and a fresh DI container per sync.

posts.title: A Dynamic Background Service Manager in .NET 8: Start, Update and Stop Workers at Runtime
posts.excerpt: How a small .NET 8 console app runs any number of named background workers, each with its own interval and config, and lets you start, retune and stop them while it runs, using async loops, CancellationToken and a ConcurrentDictionary.
posts.content:
Most .NET background work is fixed when the app starts: you register a BackgroundService and it runs until shutdown. This project takes a different approach: a small .NET 8 console app that starts, reconfigures and stops any number of named background workers while it is running, from simple typed commands.

1. What It Does

The app prints a prompt and accepts five commands:

  • START <id> <interval-ms> <config> starts a new worker that runs every interval milliseconds with its own config value.
  • UPDATE <id> <interval-ms> <config> changes a running worker's interval and config without restarting it.
  • STOP <id> cancels one worker.
  • LIST shows every running worker and its current settings.
  • EXIT quits.

That makes the number and pace of workers data, not code, which suits per-tenant pollers, sync jobs you switch on and off, or scheduled tasks whose frequency changes at runtime.

2. How the Code Is Organised

Three files, each with one job:

Service&Instances/
├── Program.cs          console loop: reads and parses commands
├── Service.cs          MyBackgroundService + ConfigData: one worker
└── ServiceManager.cs   BackgroundServiceManager: owns all workers

3. The Worker: MyBackgroundService

Each worker carries its settings in a small ConfigData class: how often to run, and a custom value standing in for whatever real settings a job would need.

public class ConfigData
{
    public int Interval { get; set; } = 5000;  // Default interval in milliseconds
    public string CustomValue { get; set; } = "DefaultConfig";
}

The worker itself is an async loop. It does its work (here, a log line), then waits for the interval with Task.Delay, and repeats until its CancellationTokenSource is cancelled:

private CancellationTokenSource _cts;
private string _serviceId;
private ConfigData _config;

public MyBackgroundService(string serviceId, ConfigData config)
{
    _serviceId = serviceId;
    _config = config;
    _cts = new CancellationTokenSource();
}

public async Task StartAsync()
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Service {_serviceId} started. Interval: {_config.Interval} ms, Config: {_config.CustomValue}");

    while (!_cts.Token.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Service {_serviceId} is running with config: {_config.CustomValue}");
        await Task.Delay(_config.Interval, _cts.Token);
    }

    Console.WriteLine($"Service {_serviceId} stopped.");
}

public void Stop()
{
    _cts.Cancel();
}

public void UpdateConfig(ConfigData newConfig)
{
    _config = newConfig;
    Console.WriteLine($"Service {_serviceId} updated: Interval={_config.Interval} ms, Config={_config.CustomValue}");
}

[!tip] Three details make it work

  • Cancellation instead of flags. The loop checks _cts.Token.IsCancellationRequested, and the same token is passed to Task.Delay, so Stop() also interrupts a worker that is in the middle of waiting.
  • Config is read on every pass. UpdateConfig just replaces _config. The loop reads _config each time round, so the next pass picks up the new value and interval.
  • Async, not threads. While a worker waits it holds no thread, so hundreds of workers cost almost nothing when idle.

4. The Manager: BackgroundServiceManager

The manager owns all workers in a ConcurrentDictionary keyed by id. Each entry stores the worker together with its current config, so LIST can report settings without asking every worker.

public class BackgroundServiceManager
{
    private readonly ConcurrentDictionary<string, (MyBackgroundService, ConfigData)> _services;

    public BackgroundServiceManager()
    {
        _services = new ConcurrentDictionary<string, (MyBackgroundService, ConfigData)>();
    }

    public string StartService(string serviceId, ConfigData config)
    {
        if (_services.ContainsKey(serviceId))
        {
            return $"Service {serviceId} is already running.";
        }

        var service = new MyBackgroundService(serviceId, config);
        _services.TryAdd(serviceId, (service, config));

        Task.Run(() => service.StartAsync());

        return $"Service {serviceId} started.";
    }

    public string StopService(string serviceId)
    {
        if (_services.TryRemove(serviceId, out var serviceTuple))
        {
            serviceTuple.Item1.Stop();
            return $"Service {serviceId} stopped.";
        }

        return $"Service {serviceId} not found.";
    }

    public string UpdateServiceConfig(string serviceId, ConfigData newConfig)
    {
        if (_services.TryGetValue(serviceId, out var serviceTuple))
        {
            serviceTuple.Item1.UpdateConfig(newConfig);
            _services[serviceId] = (serviceTuple.Item1, newConfig); // Update config in dictionary
            return $"Service {serviceId} updated with new config.";
        }

        return $"Service {serviceId} not found.";
    }

    public Dictionary<string, ConfigData> GetRunningServices()
    {
        return _services.ToDictionary(k => k.Key, v => v.Value.Item2);
    }
}
  • StartService refuses a duplicate id, creates the worker, records it, and starts its loop on the thread pool with Task.Run. It returns straight away, so the prompt stays responsive.
  • StopService removes the entry and cancels the worker in one step with TryRemove.
  • UpdateServiceConfig pushes the new config into the running worker and updates the stored copy.
  • GetRunningServices returns a snapshot, a plain dictionary copy, so the caller can loop over it while workers are added or removed.

5. The Command Loop

Program.cs reads a line, splits it on spaces and switches on the first word. Each branch validates its arguments and calls the manager. Here is START:

case "START":
    if (parts.Length < 4)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Usage: START <ServiceID> <Interval(ms)> <ConfigValue>");
        break;
    }

    string serviceId = parts[1];
    if (!int.TryParse(parts[2], out int interval))
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Invalid interval.");
        break;
    }

    string configValue = parts[3];
    ConfigData config = new ConfigData { Interval = interval, CustomValue = configValue };
    Console.WriteLine(serviceManager.StartService(serviceId, config));
    break;

A typical session:

Dynamic Background Service Manager
Available Commands: START <id> <interval> <config>, STOP <id>, UPDATE <id> <interval> <config>, LIST, EXIT

Enter command: START a 1000 hello
Service a started.
Service a started. Interval: 1000 ms, Config: hello
Service a is running with config: hello
Service a is running with config: hello

Enter command: UPDATE a 200 fast
Service a updated: Interval=200 ms, Config=fast
Service a updated with new config.
Service a is running with config: fast
Service a is running with config: fast

Enter command: LIST
Running Services:
- a: Interval=200, Config=fast

Enter command: STOP a
Service a stopped.

6. Taking It Further

The console is only one front end. Ideas for a production version:

  • Expose it as an API. Register BackgroundServiceManager as a singleton in ASP.NET Core and map POST, PUT, DELETE and GET endpoints to start, update, stop and list, so other systems can control workers.
  • Stop cleanly on shutdown. An IHostedService can stop every worker when the app exits, and the manager can keep each worker's task so a stop can wait for it to finish.
  • Apply updates immediately. A new interval takes effect after the current wait ends; cancelling the current Task.Delay with a second "wake" token applies it at once.
  • Treat stopping as normal. Task.Delay throws OperationCanceledException when cancelled; catching it (with cleanup in finally) lets the worker log its own "stopped" line.
  • Guard concurrent starts. Using the return value of TryAdd as the duplicate check keeps two simultaneous STARTs from both launching a worker.
  • Persist the workers. Save ids and configs to a database so workers come back after a restart.

posts.title: How I Turned My MacBook into a Self-Hosted Vercel with Coolify, Cloudflare Tunnel & Terraform
posts.excerpt: An 8 GB M1 MacBook, a domain, and zero open router ports: building a git-push-to-deploy platform at home, and the six things that broke along the way.
posts.content:
I wanted a place to host demo apps and APIs the way Vercel does it: push to GitHub, get a live HTTPS URL. Instead of paying for a platform, I turned a 2020 M1 MacBook Pro (8 GB RAM) into one. The site you are reading right now is served from that laptop. Here is the architecture, the build, and the problems I hit on the way.

1. What the Mac Can (and Can't) Do

My first idea was to run LLMs on it. With 8 GB of unified memory, that was never going to work: the models I use are 18 to 21 GB. What an M1 is great at is the lightweight part of a platform: a build server, a reverse proxy, a handful of Next.js and .NET containers, and a couple of databases. Heavy AI inference stays on a separate GPU box.

2. The Architecture

git push ──▶ GitHub webhook ──▶ Coolify (Linux VM on the Mac)
                                   │  builds image, rolls out container
                                   ▼
Browser ─▶ app.mydomain ─▶ Cloudflare edge (HTTPS) ─▶ Tunnel ─▶ Traefik ─▶ container

Terraform ──▶ Cloudflare API  (tunnel, DNS, routing rules)
          └─▶ Coolify API     (projects, apps, databases, services)
  • Colima runs a lightweight Ubuntu VM (4 CPU / 4 GB) because Coolify needs Linux.
  • Coolify is the open-source Heroku/Vercel alternative: GitHub integration, Nixpacks/Dockerfile builds, one-click databases, rolling deploys with health checks.
  • Cloudflare Tunnel makes an outbound-only connection to Cloudflare. No port forwarding, no static IP, free HTTPS, and my home IP is never exposed.
  • Terraform describes the whole thing as code: the tunnel, a wildcard DNS record, and every app.

3. Wildcard Routing: One Rule for Every App

The trick that makes it feel like a PaaS is a single wildcard DNS record pointing at the tunnel, with the tunnel sending everything to Coolify's Traefik proxy. Traefik routes by hostname, so a new app just needs a domain in Coolify. No DNS or Cloudflare changes, ever.

resource "cloudflare_dns_record" "wildcard" {
  zone_id = var.cloudflare_zone_id
  name    = "*.mydomain.com"
  type    = "CNAME"
  content = "TUNNEL_ID.cfargotunnel.com"
  proxied = true
}

# Tunnel ingress: every subdomain goes to Traefik
{ hostname = "*.mydomain.com", service = "http://coolify-proxy:80" }

Apps themselves are Terraform resources too. The community Coolify provider can't create applications, so I drive Coolify's REST API with the generic restapi provider. Adding a site is now one map entry and a terraform apply.

4. Six Things That Broke (and the Fixes)

  • Coolify couldn't SSH into its own server. It connects to host.docker.internal, but under Colima that name points at the Mac, not the Linux VM. Pointing the server at the VM's Docker gateway IP fixed it.
  • Every https:// domain became a redirect loop or a 404. The tunnel talks plain HTTP to Traefik while Cloudflare terminates TLS. An https:// domain in Coolify makes Traefik redirect HTTP to HTTPS forever. Rule of thumb: always http://app.domain:PORT in Coolify; the visitor still gets HTTPS from Cloudflare.
  • The apex domain wouldn't route. *.domain does not match domain itself. The bare domain needs its own DNS record and tunnel rule.
  • An n8n worker crash-looped with NOAUTH. Enabling "Connect to Predefined Network" attached it to Coolify's internal network, where the hostname redis also belongs to Coolify's own password-protected Redis. Turning that setting off restored isolation and fixed the crash.
  • Terraform updates broke deployments. Coolify's create endpoint stores a GitHub repo as owner/repo, but its PATCH endpoint stores whatever you send and later prefixes github.com again.
